title: Preface
summary: Excerpt from the OSS Simple Sabotage Field Manual No. 3 (Strategic Services Provisional, 17 January 1944, signed William J. Donovan). It states the manual is doctrine for training, must be carefully controlled and not given to unauthorized hands, may be split into pamphlets by category, and is for radio broadcasts only in local cases as the theater commander directs; it cites AR 330-5 for secret documents. Contents: introduction, possible effects, motivating the saboteur, tools/targets/timing, and specific suggestions for simple sabotage. The text is mostly OCR noise.

title: 1. INTRODUCTION'

nodes.title: 1. INTRODUCTION' (intro)
nodes.summary: Introduces simple sabotage by ordinary citizens: it uses no special tools, is done individually with minimal risk of detection, and uses everyday household or workplace items (salt, nails, candles, thread) on objects the person normally accesses. A second type needs no destructive tools and works through faulty decisions and non-cooperative attitudes, exploiting the 'human element' that causes accidents and breakdowns. Potential saboteurs should learn normal workplace decision and non-cooperation patterns to exploit that margin for error.

nodes.title: 2. POSSIBLE EFFECTS
nodes.summary: Simple sabotage acts across Europe (slashing tires, draining fuel tanks, starting fires, short-circuiting electrical systems, abrading machine parts, acting stupidly) should be encouraged to increase efficiency, reduce detectability, and multiply in number. Widespread, these acts waste enemy materials, manpower, and time, creating a constant drag on the war effort. Secondary effects include harassing and demoralizing enemy administrators and police, emboldening citizen-saboteurs to undertake larger sabotage, and leading locals to identify openly with the Allied war effort and assist during invasion and occupation.

nodes.title: 3. MOTIVATING THE SABOTEUR
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a 1944 OSS-style 'Simple Sabotage' manual on motivating citizen saboteurs. Covers personal motives (anticipated gains like enemy evacuation or ouster of officials, belief in a large unseen group of saboteurs, spreading success stories and estimated participation via radio/leaflets, fostering responsibility to recruit others); encouraging destructiveness (framing as self-defense or retaliation, humor, reversing habits such as dulling tools, and that anything can be sabotaged); tailoring tactics to unskilled workers versus technicians; dissemination media (freedom radio, false leaflets, trained agents); and safety measures (avoiding detection with innocuous materials, acts attributable to many people, plausible excuses, and not lingering after acts).

nodes.title: 4. TOOLS, TARGETS. AND TIMING
nodes.summary: Guidance on simple sabotage by citizen-saboteurs: targets and timing cannot be tightly controlled, so suggestions should fit local conditions and be emphasized by underground press and propaganda at the right time. Under general conditions, acts must be detrimental to enemy materials or manpower, use everyday equipment ingeniously, stay within the saboteur's capacity (no explosives for novices), and target objects the enemy uses, such as heavy machinery and fuels, avoiding food crops without expertise. Before an offensive, focus on industrial production. During an offensive, prefer direct, immediate effects; attack transportation, communications, and critical materials like oil, fuel, tires, and food.

nodes.title: 5. SPECIFIC SUGGESTIONS FOR SIMPLE SABOTAGE
5. SPECIFIC SUGGESTIONS FOR SIMPLE SABOTAGE (intro)
nodes.summary: The text is from a historical sabotage manual's section on simple sabotage, classifying targets. For buildings, it covers fire-starting methods (candle and paper delay devices, greased string fuses, gunpowder, gasoline-soaked paper, celluloid), advice on office records destruction, janitorial neglect, dirty factories, and gas explosions. For water and miscellaneous targets, it covers sprinkler sabotage, clogging toilets and sewers with sponges and paper, short-circuiting electrical fuses with coins, and jamming building locks.

nodes.title: (2) Industrial Production: Manufacturing
nodes.summary: This excerpt from a wartime sabotage manual lists ways to disrupt industrial production and transport. It covers tools, lubrication and cooling systems, fuel, electric motors, transformers, turbines, boilers, metal production, coal mining, agriculture, and railways. Its aim is to stop or slow work, damage equipment, and waste resources. The text is a catalog of these tactics and does not provide the operational detail needed to carry them out.

nodes.title: Sabotage Methods in Metals, Mining, Agriculture, and Rail Transport
nodes.summary: Describes sabotage suggestions across production and transport: in metals, faulty furnace linings, defective casting cores, and overheated steel; in coal mining, disabling Davy lamps, ruining pneumatic picks, weakening conveyor chains, derailing mine cars, and mixing rock into coal; in agriculture, mistimed harvests, spoiled grain and produce, and feeding crops to livestock; in railways, confusing ticket issuance and misleading schedule information.

nodes.title: (6) Transportation: Railways
nodes.summary: Describes sabotage methods a saboteur could use against enemy (regime) industry and transport: in iron/steel, faulty furnace bricks, bad cores, and overheated tempering; in coal mining, extinguishing lamps, sabotaging picks, weakening conveyor chains, derailing cars, and mixing rock into coal; in agriculture, destroying crops, livestock feed, and stores; in railways, confusing passenger travel, misrouting baggage, tampering with signals and switches, damaging track, and sabotaging engines, brakes, and lubrication.

nodes.title: (7) Transportation: Automotive
nodes.summary: Army-style sabotage guidance on automotive transportation. Roads: change or misplace signposts at intersections and forks, remove danger signals, give enemy false directions and rumors about bridges and detours, damage heavily traveled roads (ruts, sand or water in concrete, diverting streams), scatter broken glass and nails. Passengers: bus and taxi drivers waste enemy time with longest routes. Vehicles: disconnect oil pump, damage ignition, batteries (filings, vinegar, plate shattering), gears (remove lubricant, loose bolts), tires (puncture, improper repair, underinflation, misalignment), and rot tire stocks with oil or chemicals.

nodes.title: (8) Transportation: Water
nodes.summary: Describes sabotage tactics against transportation and communications. Water transport: spread false reports on waterway conditions, navigate overly cautiously near locks and bridges, neglect bilge pumping, run barges aground, delay or leave open swing/draw bridges, and tamper with ship compass magnets. Cargo: handle goods carelessly, stack heavy items on light ones, cover hatches sloppily, and leave tank float valves open. Telephone: delay or misdirect calls, cut lines, make false emergency reports, and damage earphones and connections.

nodes.title: (9) Communications
nodes.summary: A wartime sabotage manual excerpt covering ways to disrupt tires, navigation and cargo handling on water transport, telephone, telegraph, mail, motion picture and radio operations, and electric power lines, all through deliberately inefficient or damaging actions by ordinary workers.

nodes.title: (10) Electric Power
nodes.summary: The text describes covert sabotage methods against an enemy's infrastructure, grouped by category: telephone and telegraph systems (disrupting switchboards, delaying or garbling messages), transportation lines, mail delays, film projection and audience disruption at propaganda screenings, radio interference, and electrical power systems and transmission lines.

nodes.title: (11) General Interference with Organizations and Production
nodes.summary: A WWII-era sabotage manual (Simple Sabotage style) listing ways to disrupt organizations and production: delaying decisions via channels, long speeches, oversized committees, reopening settled questions, and haggling over wording. It also covers manager and worker tactics such as demanding written orders, delaying deliveries, misrouting materials, poor training, and bad work habits. Office tactics include misfiling, miscopying, and spreading rumors. It further describes employee slowdowns, feigned confusion, and complaints, plus general morale-lowering tactics like irritability and boycotts.

A historical wartime sabotage manual's section on simple sabotage, classifying targets. Buildings: fire-starting devices, record destruction, janitorial neglect, gas explosions. Water and utilities: sprinkler and sewer clogging, electrical fuse shorting, lock jamming. Industry: tool, lubrication, fuel, motor, boiler and furnace tactics, plus coal mining, agriculture, and rail. Transport: roads, vehicles, water transport, cargo. Communications: telephone, telegraph, mail, film, radio, power lines. Organizations: delays, meetings, misfiling, slowdowns, morale lowering.

summary: Describes simple sabotage by ordinary citizens using everyday items, requiring no special tools, with low detection risk. Covers its effects (wasting enemy resources, demoralizing administrators, encouraging larger sabotage), motivating saboteurs, choosing targets and timing around offensives, and specific tactics across buildings, utilities, industry, transport, communications, and organizations.
